list.label: Figure 1
list.title: Where this Note sits and what it contributes
list.caption: Where this Note sits and what it contributes. The developers of Skala present it as a step towards molecule and material design driven by simulation [3]; in practice that route is high-throughput in-silico screening [1], whose other stages are shown as context only. This Note addresses the optimize and simulate stage with four open-source modules. An input structure enters the optimization module, whose Skala-1.1 geometry goes to the Hessian module and to the NMR workflow module; the molecular property module runs once the absence of imaginary frequencies is confirmed. Bottom row: what each module was validated against on C₁₀H₆ and C₁₁H₈. The NMR shieldings are computed with B3LYP and PBE0 on the Skala-1.1 geometry, and the properties are compared with ωB97M-V. Screening itself is not demonstrated here.
list.alt: Figure 1: where this Note sits in the screening route and the four open-source modules it contributes
list.section: 1.2 What is missing

list.label: Figure 2
list.title: From a rough candidate to a verified structure that the community can reuse
list.caption: From a rough candidate to a verified structure that the community can reuse. Left: the opportunity, faster discovery of new molecules, drugs and materials by simulating many candidates and sending a short list to the laboratory. Centre: the four open-source modules of this Note (optimize, verify, compare, properties), each with the question it answers and its result for C₁₀H₆ and C₁₁H₈: 16 of 18 runs reach one structure, no imaginary modes at the end points, ¹³C errors of 1.30 to 1.95 ppm against the 2.0 ppm limit, and atomic charges with R² above 0.999 against ωB97M-V. Right: the community, who can reuse the code, prompts, call logs, inputs and outputs on larger, flexible molecules with heteroatoms. The Note was tested on two synthesized annulenes; screening itself is not demonstrated here.
list.alt: Figure 2: from a rough candidate to a verified structure the community can reuse; the opportunity, the four modules with one question and one result each, and the community

list.label: Figure 4
list.title: Flowchart of the four open-source modules in detail
list.caption: Flowchart of the four open-source modules in detail. The agentic optimizer (module 1) turns a rough, strained structure into a relaxed geometry with a decision log, using a supervision loop of monitor, language-model action, guard and probation around L-BFGS. This def2-SVP geometry is the input of the Hessian module (module 2) and of the NMR workflow module (module 3). The Hessian module refines it at def2-TZVP and checks that no imaginary frequency remains; the verified minimum is the input of the molecular property module (module 4). Schematic of the workflow, not computed data.
list.alt: Figure 4: flowchart of the four open-source modules in detail

list.label: Figure 5
list.title: The agentic optimizer module couples a GFN2-xTB basin search with L-BFGS on Skala-1.1 under two Gemini models
list.caption: The agentic optimizer module couples a GFN2-xTB basin search with L-BFGS on Skala-1.1 under two Gemini models. A distorted C₁₁H₈ start (left, edge-on view) enters the module. The agentic core (shaded) is xTB plus L-BFGS together: a code-run xTB basin search supplies candidate basins, Gemini Argon chooses the starting basin, and L-BFGS on Skala-1.1 is the only step that moved atoms in the annulene runs. When a stall is detected, Gemini Flash steers L-BFGS through function calls to its tools and returns one checked action. Argon makes the final check before the relaxed, planar geometry and the decision log are returned (right, top view). A plain run is the L-BFGS box alone. Molecular views rendered with 3Dmol.js.
list.alt: Figure 5: the agentic optimizer module
list.section: 2.2 Agentic optimizer module: xTB basin search and agent-supervised L-BFGS

list.label: Figure 6
list.title: One supervision layer, selectable controller
list.caption: One supervision layer, selectable controller. The monitor, the typed actions and the guard (validator, five-step probation, rollback and switch-off) are the same for every controller. Left: the agent with advisor, which answers every event through function calls; the step advisor is one of its functions. Right: the rule-based controller, which decides without a model call, and the combined mode, in which the agent is consulted only when one of the conditions H1 to H4 holds. list.section: 2.3 Hessian module: harmonic frequencies, IR intensities and vDOS

list.label: Figure 8
list.title: The Hessian module
list.caption: The Hessian module. Top: an input geometry is optimized with L-BFGS on Skala-1.1 on a GPU; the optimized geometry then enters the harmonic analysis with Skala-1.1 on a GPU, which returns the frequencies, checked for the absence of imaginary frequencies, with a frequency-mapped molecular view, the vDOS and the IR spectrum as outputs. Bottom left: the frequency calculation as a computation graph in two parts. The Hessian part (steps 1 to 3, 10 and 11) displaces each atom, evaluates the Skala-1.1 forces on every displaced structure, assembles the Hessian from numerical differences of the forces and diagonalizes it, mass-weighted. The Skala network (steps 4 to 9) is evaluated inside every force call. Bottom right: the atoms of C₁₁H₈ (top) and C₁₀H₆ (bottom) coloured by their local atomic force-constant stiffness.
list.alt: Figure 8: the Hessian module as a block diagram and as the computation graph of the frequency calculation

list.label: Figure 17
list.title: The saddle-point trap and the ammonia test
list.caption: The saddle-point trap and the ammonia test. (A) A plain optimizer can stop on a saddle point, where the forces vanish although one direction still curves downhill; a curvature probe shows the imaginary mode, and a displacement along it lets the optimization continue to a minimum. (B) A higher local minimum is a different trap, which the two equal wells of ammonia cannot test. (C) Relaxed inversion profile of ammonia at the Skala-1.1/def2-SVP level against the height of N above the H₃ plane. Plain L-BFGS stopped on the planar saddle (7.4 kcal mol⁻¹; imaginary mode of 906 to 910 cm⁻¹ in the verifying Hessian) in 8 of 10 runs, and all six language-model runs ended in a well (the same mode real, at 1118 to 1128 cm⁻¹).
list.alt: Figure 17: the saddle-point trap and the ammonia test

list.label: Figure A1
list.title: Optimizing a molecular structure, pictured as a walk downhill
list.caption: Optimizing a molecular structure, pictured as a walk downhill.  a , The height of the landscape is the energy of the molecule, and each position is one shape of it. An optimizer starts from a rough, strained shape and moves step by step towards lower energy. A valley floor is a minimum, a stable structure. A mountain pass (saddle point) is also level, but it is not stable.  b , The step cap is the longest stride the optimizer may take. Too short, and the run crawls. Too long, and a strained molecule may be torn apart. Schematic, not computed data.
list.alt: Figure A1: the walk downhill, an energy landscape with a start, a valley floor and a mountain pass, and three step lengths
list.section: Appendix figures

list.label: Figure A2
list.title: An optimizer with a supervising agent and safeguards
list.caption: An optimizer with a supervising agent and safeguards. The optimizer makes every step, and plain code checks each one. Most steps need no action. When progress stalls, an AI agent (a large language model) suggests one change to the optimizer settings. A validator checks the change against fixed limits. An accepted change runs for five trial steps from a checkpoint, and it is rolled back if the run has become worse. Every request, answer and decision is saved. The agent changes settings only and never moves the atoms. Schematic; the full sequence is in figure A5.
list.alt: Figure A2: a loop in which an optimizer, a monitor, an AI agent, a validator and a trial period work together, with a logbook

list.label: Figure A5
list.title: Sequence of one supervised step
list.caption: Sequence of one supervised step. After every L-BFGS step on Skala-1.1 the monitor looks for a stall trigger. If one fires, the controller asks the Gemini model, which may call tools (up to six rounds) and submits one action; the validator checks bounds, evidence and plausibility. An accepted change runs for five probation steps and is rolled back if the energy or the largest force is worse than at the checkpoint; after two failed actions the agent is switched off and the baseline schedule is restored.

The supervised run reached the force target at step 65 and finished at step 82. The plain run on the weak hand schedule ("baseline") reached the target at step 124, and the plain run on the random schedule did not reach it within its 147 steps. The runs are single runs of two set-ups that also differ in L-BFGS memory and warm start, so the step counts printed in the image are not the effect of the agent alone and no speed-up is claimed from them; the like-for-like test is the sweep of table S3.1.

fig01.label: Figure 1
fig01.title: Where this Note sits and what it contributes
fig01.caption: Where this Note sits and what it contributes. The developers of Skala present it as a step towards molecule and material design driven by simulation [3]; in practice that route is high-throughput in-silico screening [1], whose other stages are shown as context only. This Note addresses the optimize and simulate stage with four open-source modules. An input structure enters the optimization module, whose Skala-1.1 geometry goes to the Hessian module and to the NMR workflow module; the molecular property module runs once the absence of imaginary frequencies is confirmed. Bottom row: what each module was validated against on C₁₀H₆ and C₁₁H₈. The NMR shieldings are computed with B3LYP and PBE0 on the Skala-1.1 geometry, and the properties are compared with ωB97M-V. Screening itself is not demonstrated here.
fig01.alt: Figure 1: where this Note sits in the screening route and the four open-source modules it contributes

fig02.label: Figure 2
fig02.title: From a rough candidate to a verified structure that the community can reuse
fig02.caption: From a rough candidate to a verified structure that the community can reuse. Left: the opportunity, faster discovery of new molecules, drugs and materials by simulating many candidates and sending a short list to the laboratory. Centre: the four open-source modules of this Note (optimize, verify, compare, properties), each with the question it answers and its result for C₁₀H₆ and C₁₁H₈: 16 of 18 runs reach one structure, no imaginary modes at the end points, ¹³C errors of 1.30 to 1.95 ppm against the 2.0 ppm limit, and atomic charges with R² above 0.999 against ωB97M-V. Right: the community, who can reuse the code, prompts, call logs, inputs and outputs on larger, flexible molecules with heteroatoms. The Note was tested on two synthesized annulenes; screening itself is not demonstrated here.

figA01.label: Figure A1
figA01.title: Optimizing a molecular structure, pictured as a walk downhill
figA01.caption: Optimizing a molecular structure, pictured as a walk downhill.  a , The height of the landscape is the energy of the molecule, and each position is one shape of it. An optimizer starts from a rough, strained shape and moves step by step towards lower energy. A valley floor is a minimum, a stable structure. A mountain pass (saddle point) is also level, but it is not stable.  b , The step cap is the longest stride the optimizer may take. Too short, and the run crawls. Too long, and a strained molecule may be torn apart. Schematic, not computed data.

figA02.label: Figure A2
figA02.title: An optimizer with a supervising agent and safeguards
figA02.caption: An optimizer with a supervising agent and safeguards. The optimizer makes every step, and plain code checks each one. Most steps need no action. When progress stalls, an AI agent (a large language model) suggests one change to the optimizer settings. A validator checks the change against fixed limits. An accepted change runs for five trial steps from a checkpoint, and it is rolled back if the run has become worse. Every request, answer and decision is saved. The agent changes settings only and never moves the atoms. Schematic; the full sequence is in figure A5.
figA02.alt: Figure A2: a loop in which an optimizer, a monitor, an AI agent, a validator and a trial period work together, with a logbook

figA03.caption: The integrated workflow. The four open-source modules contributed by this Note are shown with the main steps of each. Schematic of the workflow, not computed data.
